quotes.text: "You are blubbering again, little milksop! If you don't want to go, stay behind; no one is taking you by force!  Never mind, never mind, Yegor boy, never mind,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "never mind, my boy. . . . Call upon God. . . . You are not going for your harm, but for your good. Learning is light, as the saying is, and ignorance is darkness. . . . That is so, truly."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, you'd better go back then. Anyway, you are going for nothing; it's a day's journey for a spoonful of porridge."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Call upon God. . . . Lomonosov set off with the fishermen in the same way, and he became a man famous all over Europe. Learning in conjunction with faith brings forth fruit pleasing to God. What are the words of the prayer? For the glory of our Maker, for the comfort of our parents, for the benefit of our Church and our country. . . . Yes, indeed!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The benefit is not the same in all cases,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "some will study twenty years and get no sense from it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Learning is a benefit to some, but others only muddle their brains. My sister is a woman who does not understand; she is set upon refinement, and wants to turn Yegorka into a learned man, and she does not understand that with my business I could settle Yegorka happily for the rest of his life. I tell you this, that if everyone were to go in for being learned and refined there would be no one to sow the corn and do the trading; they would all die of hunger."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And if all go in for trading and sowing corn there will be no one to acquire learning."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What a swollen lump of a face, as though a bumble-bee had stung it!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, Deniska, shall we overtake the waggons to-day?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "By nightfall, please God, we shall overtake them."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Did Varlamov come this way yesterday or not?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A fine windmill Boltva has put up for his son,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And how is it we don't see his farm?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is that way, beyond the creek."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I studied too, my boy; from the earliest age God instilled into me good sense and understanding, so that while I was just such a lad as you I was beyond others, a comfort to my parents and preceptors by my good sense. Before I was fifteen I could speak and make verses in Latin, just as in Russian. I was the crosier-bearer to his Holiness Bishop Christopher. After mass one day, as I remember it was the patron saint's day of His Majesty Tsar Alexandr Pavlovitch of blessed memory, he unrobed at the altar, looked kindly at me and asked, 'Puer bone, quam appelaris?' And I answered, 'Christopherus sum;' and he said, 'Ergo connominati sumus'-- that is, that we were namesakes. . . Then he asked in Latin, 'Whose son are you?' To which I answered, also in Latin, that I was the son of deacon Sireysky of the village of Lebedinskoe. Seeing my readiness and the clearness of my answers, his Holiness blessed me and said, 'Write to your father that I will not forget him, and that I will keep you in view.' The holy priests and fathers who were standing round the altar, hearing our discussion in Latin, were not a little surprised, and everyone expressed his pleasure in praise of me. Before I had moustaches, my boy, I could read Latin, Greek, and French; I knew philosophy, mathematics, secular history, and all the sciences. The Lord gave me a marvellous memory. Sometimes, if I read a thing once or twice, I knew it by heart. My preceptors and patrons were amazed, and so they expected I should make a learned man, a luminary of the Church. I did think of going to Kiev to continue my studies, but my parents did not approve. 'You'll be studying all your life,' said my father; 'when shall we see you finished?' Hearing such words, I gave up study and took a post. . . . Of course, I did not become a learned man, but then I did not disobey my parents; I was a comfort to them in their old age and gave them a creditable funeral. Obedience is more than fasting and prayer.  I suppose you have forgotten all your learning?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I should think so! Thank God, I have reached my eightieth year! Something of philosophy and rhetoric I do remember, but languages and mathematics I have quite forgotten."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What is a substance? A creature is a self-existing object, not requiring anything else for its completion."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Of a truth matter nourishes the flesh and spiritual nourishment the soul!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "but if we don't overtake Varlamov, learning won't do much for us."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A man isn't a needle-- we shall find him. He must be going his rounds in these parts."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Deniska, where are you? Come and eat,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am going to sleep, and you mind that no one takes the sack from under my head."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You look out that no one takes away the horses!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I say, which of us will get to the sedge first?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Father Christopher, get up; it is time to start,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Wake up; we've slept too long as it is! Deniska, put the horses in."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "it's time to start; the horses are ready, and here are you, . . . upon my word."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I must read the psalms. . . . I haven't read them to-day."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ivan Ivanitch, that is my rule every day. . . . I can't . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Hallelujah, hallelujah, hallelujah! Glory be to Thee, O Lord!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What a happy day for me! Oh, what am I to do now? Ivan Ivanitch! Father Christopher! What a pretty little gentleman sitting on the box, God strike me dead! Oh, my goodness! why am I standing here instead of asking the visitors indoors? Please walk in, I humbly beg you. . . . You are kindly welcome! Give me all your things. . . . Oh, my goodness me!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ivan Ivanitch and Father Christopher have come,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Dear, dear! What a surprise! Such honoured guests to have come us so suddenly! Come, take their things, Solomon. Walk in, honoured guests."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "One party went by early this morning, and the other, Ivan Ivanitch, put up here for dinner and went on towards evening."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ah! . . . Has Varlamov been by or not?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, Ivan Ivanitch. His clerk, Grigory Yegoritch, went by yesterday morning and said that he had to be to-day at the Molokans' farm."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Good! so we will go after the waggons directly and then on to the Molokans'."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Where are you going for the night? You will have a nice little supper and stay the night, and to-morrow morning, please God, you can go on and overtake anyone you like."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There is no time for that. . . . Excuse me, Moisey Moisevitch, another time; but now I must make haste. We'll stay a quarter of an hour and then go on; we can stay the night at the Molokans'."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Have you no fear of God, Ivan Ivanitch? You will compel me to hide your caps and lock the door! You must have a cup of tea and a snack of something, anyway."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ivan Ivanitch! Father Christopher! Do be so good as to take a cup of tea with me. Surely I am not such a bad man that you can't even drink tea in my house? Ivan Ivanitch!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, we may just as well have a cup of tea,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Solomon, why did you not come to our fair at N. this summer, and act some Jewish scenes?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wish you a good appetite! Tea and sugar!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I hope you will enjoy it. Such rare guests, such rare ones; it is years since I last saw Father Christopher. And will no one tell me who is this nice little gentleman?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is the son of my sister, Olga Ivanovna,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To school. We are taking him to a high school."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That's a fine thing. You will come back from the high school such a gentleman that we shall all take off our hats to you. You will be wealthy and wise and so grand that your mamma will be delighted. Oh, that's a fine thing!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You must excuse me, Father Christopher, but I am thinking of writing to the bishop to tell him you are robbing the merchants of their living. I shall take a sheet of stamped paper and write that I suppose Father Christopher is short of pence, as he has taken up with trade and begun selling wool."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "H'm, yes . . . it's a queer notion in my old age,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have turned from priest to merchant, brother. I ought to be at home now saying my prayers, instead of galloping about the country like a Pharaoh in his chariot. . . . Vanity!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But it will mean a lot of pence!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, I dare say! More kicks than halfpence, and serve me right. The wool's not mine, but my son-in-law MikhailÕs!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why, because . . . His mother's milk is scarcely dry upon his lips. He can buy wool all right, but when it comes to selling, he has no sense; he is young yet. He has wasted all his money; he wanted to grow rich and cut a dash, but he tried here and there, and no one would give him his price. And so the lad went on like that for a year, and then he came to me and said, 'Daddy, you sell the wool for me; be kind and do it! I am no good at the business!' And that is true enough. As soon as there is anything wrong then it's 'Daddy,' but till then they could get on without their dad. When he was buying he did not consult me, but now when he is in difficulties it's Daddy's turn. And what does his dad know about it? If it were not for Ivan Ivanitch, his dad could do nothing. I have a lot of worry with them."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes; one has a lot of worry with one's children, I can tell you that,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have six of my own. One needs schooling, another needs doctoring, and a third needs nursing, and when they grow up they are more trouble still. It is not only nowadays, it was the same in Holy Scripture. When Jacob had little children he wept, and when they grew up he wept still more bitterly."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have no cause myself to rail against the Lord. I have lived to the end of my days as any man might be thankful to live. . . . I have married my daughters to good men, my sons I have set up in life, and now I am free; I have done my work and can go where I like. I live in peace with my wife. I eat and drink and sleep and rejoice in my grandchildren, and say my prayers and want nothing more. I live on the fat of the land, and don't need to curry favour with anyone. I have never had any trouble from childhood, and now suppose the Tsar were to ask me, 'What do you need? What would you like?' why, I don't need anything. I have everything I want and everything to be thankful for. In the whole town there is no happier man than I am. My only trouble is I have so many sins, but there --only God is without sin. That's right, isn't it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have no teeth, of course; my poor old back aches; there is one thing and another, . . . asthma and that sort of thing. . . . I ache. . . . The flesh is weak, but then think of my age! I am in the eighties! One can't go on for ever; one mustn't outstay one's welcome."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My eldest son Gavrila came to pay me a visit. He is in the medical line, and is a district doctor in the province of Tchernigov. . . . 'Very well . . .' I said to him, 'here I have asthma and one thing and another. . . . You are a doctor; cure your father!' He undressed me on the spot, tapped me, listened, and all sorts of tricks, . . . kneaded my stomach, and then he said, 'Dad, you ought to be treated with compressed air.'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And I said to him, 'God bless your compressed air!'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Let me get my breath . . . . You'll be the death of me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "While we have the time, Father Christopher, let us reckon up,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How many are there in the rolls of roubles?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The rouble notes are done up in fifties, . . . the three-rouble notes in nineties, the twenty-five and hundred roubles in thousands. You count out seven thousand eight hundred for Varlamov, and I will count out for Gusevitch. And mind you don't make a mistake. . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You bring trouble! Now I expect my Mihailo is asleep and dreaming that I am going to bring him a heap of money like this."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your Mihailo Timofevitch is a man who doesn't understand business,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "he undertakes what isn't his work, but you understand and can judge. You had better hand over your wool to me, as I have said already, and I would give you half a rouble above my own price-- yes, I would, simply out of regard for you. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I thank you for your kindness. . . . Of course, if it were for me to decide, I shouldn't think twice about it; but as it is, the wool is not mine, as you know. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "come and see the little bear I can show you! Such a queer, cross little bear. Oo-oo!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are here without your mamma, and no one to look after you. Eat it up."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And how many brothers and sisters have you got?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am the only one; there are no others."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Poor mamma, poor mamma! How she will weep and miss you! We are going to send our Nahum to school in a year. O-oh!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "you have no mamma now-- no one to give you nice things."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What sort of business are you talking about?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, things in general. What are you doing?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The same as everyone else. . . . You see, I am a menial, I am my brother's servant; my brother's the servant of the visitors; the visitors are Varlamov's servants; and if I had ten millions, Varlamov would be my servant."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why, because there isn't a gentleman or millionaire who isn't ready to lick the hand of a scabby Jew for the sake of making a kopeck. Now, I am a scabby Jew and a beggar. Everybody looks at me as though I were a dog, but if I had money Varlamov would play the fool before me just as Moisey does before you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How can you compare yourself with Varlamov, you blockhead?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am not such a fool as to put myself on a level with Varlamov,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Though Varlamov is a Russian, he is at heart a scabby Jew; money and gain are all he lives for, but I threw my money in the stove! I don't want money, or land, or sheep, and there is no need for people to be afraid of me and to take off their hats when I pass. So I am wiser than your Varlamov and more like a man!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If you don't like your religion you had better change it, but to laugh at it is a sin; it is only the lowest of the low who will make fun of his religion."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am talking of one thing and you are talking of something else. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "One can see you are a foolish fellow,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I admonish you to the best of my ability, and you are angry. I speak to you like an old man quietly, and you answer like a turkeycock: 'Bla-- bla-- bla!' You really are a queer fellow. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What a ferocious fellow you've got here, Moisey Moisevitch! God bless him!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You ought to find him a place or a wife or something. . . . There's no knowing what to make of him. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He's rude and thinks too much of himself."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Be so kind as to excuse it, and don't be angry. He is such a queer fellow, such a queer fellow! Oh dear, oh dear! He is my own brother, but I have never had anything but trouble from him. You know he's. . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is not in his right mind; . . . he's hopeless. And I don't know what I am to do with him! He cares for nobody, he respects nobody, and is afraid of nobody. . . . You know he laughs at everybody, he says silly things, speaks familiarly to anyone. You wouldn't believe it, Varlamov came here one day and Solomon said such things to him that he gave us both a taste of his whip. . . . But why whip me? Was it my fault? God has robbed him of his wits, so it is God's will, and how am I to blame?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He does not sleep at night, and is always thinking and thinking and thinking, and what he is thinking about God only knows. If you go to him at night he is angry and laughs. He doesn't like me either . . . . And there is nothing he wants! When our father died he left us each six thousand roubles. I bought myself an inn, married, and now I have children; and he burnt all his money in the stove. Such a pity, such a pity! Why burn it? If he didn't want it he could give it to me, but why burn it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your Excellency must excuse us for not being tidy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If you see him to-morrow, ask him to come and see me for a minute."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Whose boy is it? Kazimir Mihalovitch, look what a charming fellow! Good heavens, he is asleep!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Get up; it is time to start."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But doesn't that Kazimir Mihalovitch plunder her right and left! The year before last when, do you remember, I bought some wool from her, he made over three thousand from my purchase alone."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is just what you would expect from a Pole,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And little does it trouble her. Young and foolish, as they say, her head is full of nonsense."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Woa! Good-evening, Panteley! Is everything all right?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "First-rate, Ivan Ivanitch!  Haven't you seen Varlamov, lads?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, then, we shall go on to the Molokans'!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The Jew told us that Varlamov was putting up for the night at the Molokans'. So good-bye, lads! Good luck to you!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "you take my little lad along with you! Why should he go jolting off with us for nothing? You put him on the bales, Panteley, and let him come on slowly, and we shall overtake you. Get down, Yegor! Go on; it's all right. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't be unkind to him, you devils!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ah, you are awake, youngster! So you are the son of Ivan Ivanitch?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nephew of Ivan Ivanitch? Here I have taken off my boots and am hopping along barefoot. My feet are bad; they are swollen, and it's easier without my boots . . . easier, youngster . . . without boots, I mean. . . . So you are his nephew? He is a good man; no harm in him. . . . God give him health. . . . No harm in him . . . I mean Ivan Ivanitch. . . . He has gone to the Molokans'. . . . O Lord, have mercy upon us!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To school? Aha! . . . Well, may the Queen of Heaven help you. Yes. One brain is good, but two are better. To one man God gives one brain, to another two brains, and to another three. . . . To another three, that is true. . . . One brain you are born with, one you get from learning, and a third with a good life. So you see, my lad, it is a good thing if a man has three brains. Living is easier for him, and, what's more, dying is, too. Dying is, too. . . . And we shall all die for sure."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Maxim Nikolaitch, the gentleman from Slavyanoserbsk, brought a little lad to school, too, last year. I don't know how he is getting on there in studying the sciences, but he was a nice good little lad. . . . God give them help, they are nice gentlemen. Yes, he, too, brought his boy to school. . . . In Slavyanoserbsk there is no establishment, I suppose, for study. No. . . . But it is a nice town. . . . There's an ordinary school for simple folks, but for the higher studies there is nothing. No, that's true. What's your name? . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yegory, then. . . . The holy martyr Yegory, the Bearer of Victory, whose day is the twenty-third of April. And my christian name is Panteley, . . . Panteley Zaharov Holodov. . . . We are Holodovs . . . . I am a native of-- maybe you've heard of it-- Tim in the province of Kursk. My brothers are artisans and work at trades in the town, but I am a peasant. . . . I have remained a peasant. Seven years ago I went there-- home, I mean. I went to the village and to the town. . . . To Tim, I mean. Then, thank God, they were all alive and well; . . . but now I don't know. . . . Maybe some of them are dead. . . . And it's time they did die, for some of them are older than I am. Death is all right; it is good so long, of course, as one does not die without repentance. There is no worse evil than an impenitent death; an impenitent death is a joy to the devil. And if you want to die penitent, so that you may not be forbidden to enter the mansions of the Lord, pray to the holy martyr Varvara. She is the intercessor. She is, that's the truth. . . . For God has given her such a place in the heavens that everyone has the right to pray to her for penitence."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, he took his little lad; . . . he took him, that's true . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I say, lads, Dymov has killed a snake!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That's not a viper; it's a grass snake!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What have you killed a grass snake for? What had he done to you, you damned brute? Look, he has killed a grass snake; how would you like to be treated so?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Grass snakes ought not to be killed, that's true,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "they ought not. . . They are not vipers; though it looks like a snake, it is a gentle, innocent creature. . . . It's friendly to man, the grass snake is."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Grandfather, what did he want to kill the grass snake for?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Grandfather, what did he kill it for?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A stupid fellow. His hands itch to kill, and that is why he does it,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "but he oughtn't to kill a grass snake, that's true. . . . Dymov is a ruffian, we all know, he kills everything he comes across, and Kiruha did not interfere. He ought to have taken its part, but instead of that, he goes off into 'Ha-ha-ha!' and 'Ho-ho-ho!' . . . But don't be angry, Vassya. . . . Why be angry? They've killed it-- well, never mind them. Dymov is a ruffian and Kiruha acted from foolishness-- never mind. . . . They are foolish people without understanding-- but there, don't mind them. Emelyan here never touches what he shouldn't; he never does; . . . that is true, . . . because he is a man of education, while they are stupid. . . . Emelyan, he doesn't touch things."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "So I have been saying things to him to stop his being angry. . . . Oh, how my swollen feet hurt! Oh, oh! They are more inflamed than ever for Sunday, God's holy day!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, lad, no. It's not from walking. When I walk it seems easier; when I lie down and get warm, . . . it's deadly. Walking is easier for me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have no voice. It's a real misfortune. All last night and this morning I have been haunted by the trio 'Lord, have Mercy' that we sang at the wedding at Marionovsky's. It's in my head and in my throat. It seems as though I could sing it, but I can't; I have no voice."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "For fifteen years I was in the choir. In all the Lugansky works there was, maybe, no one with a voice like mine. But, confound it, I bathed two years ago in the Donets, and I can't get a single note true ever since. I took cold in my throat. And without a voice I am like a workman without hands."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I think of myself as a ruined man and nothing more."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There's a little gentleman driving with us,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What a grand driver! Stay with us and you shall drive the waggons and sell wool."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I say, lads, the old man has been brought to bed of a boy in the night!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Grandfather, why do you drink out of a lamp?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "One man drinks out of a pail and another out of a lamp,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Every man to his own taste. . . . You drink out of the pail-- well, drink, and may it do you good. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Who is it you are talking to?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A darling fox, . . . lying on her back, playing like a dog."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Fool! I'll punch you in the face."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You blackguard! You son of a bitch!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ha-ha-ha! Let us catch fish! Mates, let us catch fish."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "there must be a lot of fish here."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Styopka, run to the village and ask the peasants for a net!  They won't give it to me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They will, you ask them. Tell them that they should give it to us for Christ's sake, because we are just the same as pilgrims."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How is it your chin is swollen?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's bad. . . . I used to work at the match factory, little sir. . . . The doctor used to say that it would make my jaw rot. The air is not healthy there. There were three chaps beside me who had their jaws swollen, and with one of them it rotted away altogether."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are only frightening the fish, you stupids! Go more to the left! It's shallower there!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You've let the perch slip! It's gone!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Look at this perch! We've five like that!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Vassya is eating a live gudgeon! Phoo!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's not a gudgeon, but a minnow,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, don't trouble yourself to thank me; I don't like it . . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Have they given out the holy bread?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Just wait a minute; I will give it you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Give me a farthing's worth of sunflower seeds,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And how much do you charge for cakes like this?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There are all sorts of Ivan Ivanitchs,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Those are not oats, but chaff. It's a mockery to give that to the hens; enough to make the hens laugh. . . . No, I will go to Bondarenko."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No need. The fish will make its own gravy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You there! Give the little lad a spoon!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I dare say he is hungry too!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Peasant fare is welcome, too, when one is hungry."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You can't eat with your cap on, and you a gentleman too!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Are we going to start soon, grandfather?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In God's good time we shall set off. There's no starting yet; it is too hot. . . . O Lord, Thy will be done. Holy Mother. . . Lie down, little lad."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Took his little lad to school-- but how he is doing now I haven't heard say --in Slavyanoserbsk. I say there is no establishment for teaching them to be very clever. . . . No, that's true -- a nice little lad, no harm in him. . . . He'll grow up and be a help to his father. . . . You, Yegory, are little now, but you'll grow big and will keep your father and mother. . . . So it is ordained of God, 'Honour your father and your mother.' . . . I had children myself, but they were burnt. . . . My wife was burnt and my children, . . . that's true. . . . The hut caught fire on the night of Epiphany. . . . I was not at home, I was driving in Oryol. In Oryol. . . . Marya dashed out into the street, but remembering that the children were asleep in the hut, ran back and was burnt with her children. . . . Next day they found nothing but bones."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nikola, isn't this the place where the mowers killed the merchants?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Two merchants, father and son, were travelling, selling holy images. They put up in the inn not far from here that is now kept by Ignat Fomin. The old man had a drop too much, and began boasting that he had a lot of money with him. We all know merchants are a boastful set, God preserve us. . . . They can't resist showing off before the likes of us. And at the time some mowers were staying the night at the inn. So they overheard what the merchants said and took note of it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Next day, as soon as it was light,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "the merchants were preparing to set off and the mowers tried to join them. 'Let us go together, your worships. It will be more cheerful and there will be less danger, for this is an out-of-the-way place. . . .' The merchants had to travel at a walking pace to avoid breaking the images, and that just suited the mowers. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Everything went all right till they reached this spot, and then the mowers let fly at them with their scythes. The son, he was a fine young fellow, snatched the scythe from one of them, and he used it, too. . . . Well, of course, they got the best of it because there were eight of them. They hacked at the merchants so that there was not a sound place left on their bodies; when they had finished they dragged both of them off the road, the father to one side and the son to the other. Opposite that cross there is another cross on this side. . . . Whether it is still standing, I don't know. . . . I can't see from here. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They say they did not find much money afterwards."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And three of them died afterwards, for the merchant had cut them badly with the scythe, too. They died from loss of blood. One had his hand cut off, so that they say he ran three miles without his hand, and they found him on a mound close to Kurikovo. He was squatting on his heels, with his head on his knees, as though he were lost in thought, but when they looked at him there was no life in him and he was dead. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They found him by the track of blood,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There are a great many wicked people in the world,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I've seen lots and lots of them. . . . Wicked people! . . . I have seen a great many holy and just, too. . . . Queen of Heaven, save us and have mercy on us. I remember once thirty years ago, or maybe more, I was driving a merchant from Morshansk. The merchant was a jolly handsome fellow, with money, too . . . the merchant was . . . a nice man, no harm in him. . . . So we put up for the night at an inn. And in Russia the inns are not what they are in these parts. There the yards are roofed in and look like the ground floor, or let us say like barns in good farms. Only a barn would be a bit higher. So we put up there and were all right. My merchant was in a room, while I was with the horses, and everything was as it should be. So, lads, I said my prayers before going to sleep and began walking about the yard. And it was a dark night, I couldn't see anything; it was no good trying. So I walked about a bit up to the waggons, or nearly, when I saw a light gleaming. What could it mean? I thought the people of the inn had gone to bed long ago, and besides the merchant and me there were no other guests in the inn. . . . Where could the light have come from? I felt suspicious. . . . I went closer . . . towards the light. . . . The Lord have mercy upon me! and save me, Queen of Heaven! I looked and there was a little window with a grating, . . . close to the ground, in the house. . . I lay down on the ground and looked in; as soon as I looked in a cold chill ran all down me. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I looked in and there was a big cellar, black and dark. . . . There was a lighted lantern on a tub. In the middle of the cellar were about a dozen men in red shirts with their sleeves turned up, sharpening long knives. . . . Ugh! So we had fallen into a nest of robbers. . . . What's to be done? I ran to the merchant, waked him up quietly, and said: 'Don't be frightened, merchant,' said I, 'but we are in a bad way. We have fallen into a nest of robbers,' I said. He turned pale and asked: 'What are we to do now, Panteley? I have a lot of money that belongs to orphans. As for my life,' he said, 'that's in God's hands. I am not afraid to die, but it's dreadful to lose the orphans' money,' said he. . . . What were we to do? The gates were locked; there was no getting out. If there had been a fence one could have climbed over it, but with the yard shut up! . . . 'Come, don't be frightened, merchant,' said I; 'but pray to God. Maybe the Lord will not let the orphans suffer. Stay still.' said I, 'and make no sign, and meanwhile, maybe, I shall think of something. . . .' Right! . . . I prayed to God and the Lord put the thought into my mind. . . . I clambered up on my chaise and softly, . . . softly so that no one should hear, began pulling out the straw in the thatch, made a hole and crept out, crept out. . . . Then I jumped off the roof and ran along the road as fast as I could. I ran and ran till I was nearly dead. . . . I ran maybe four miles without taking breath, if not more. Thank God I saw a village. I ran up to a hut and began tapping at a window. 'Good Christian people,' I said, and told them all about it, 'do not let a Christian soul perish. . . .' I waked them all up. . . . The peasants gathered together and went with me, . . one with a cord, one with an oakstick, others with pitchforks. . . . We broke in the gates of the inn-yard and went straight to the cellar. . . . And the robbers had just finished sharpening their knives and were going to kill the merchant. The peasants took them, every one of them, bound them and carried them to the police. The merchant gave them three hundred roubles in his joy, and gave me five gold pieces and put my name down. They said that they found human bones in the cellar afterwards, heaps and heaps of them. . . . Bones! . . . So they robbed people and then buried them, so that there should be no traces. . . . Well, afterwards they were punished at Morshansk."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I went another journey with a merchant, too, . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "His name, as I remember now, was Pyotr Grigoritch. He was a nice man, . . . the merchant was. We stopped in the same way at an inn. . . . He indoors and me with the horses. . . . The people of the house, the innkeeper and his wife, seemed friendly good sort of people; the labourers, too, seemed all right; but yet, lads, I couldn't sleep. I had a queer feeling in my heart, . . . a queer feeling, that was just it. The gates were open and there were plenty of people about, and yet I felt afraid and not myself. Everyone had been asleep long ago. It was the middle of the night; it would soon be time to get up, and I was lying alone in my chaise and could not close my eyes, as though I were some owl. And then, lads, I heard this sound, 'Toop! toop! toop!' Someone was creeping up to the chaise. I poke my head out, and there was a peasant woman in nothing but her shift and with her feet bare. . . . 'What do you want, good woman?' I asked. And she was all of a tremble; her face was terror-stricken. . . 'Get up, good man,' said she; 'the people are plotting evil. . . . They mean to kill your merchant. With my own ears I heard the master whispering with his wife. . . .' So it was not for nothing, the foreboding of my heart! 'And who are you?' I asked. 'I am their cook,' she said. . . . Right! . . . So I got out of the chaise and went to the merchant. I waked him up and said: 'Things aren't quite right, Pyotr Grigoritch. . . . Make haste and rouse yourself from sleep, your worship, and dress now while there is still time,' I said; 'and to save our skins, let us get away from trouble.' He had no sooner begun dressing when the door opened and, mercy on us! I saw, Holy Mother! the innkeeper and his wife come into the room with three labourers. . . . So they had persuaded the labourers to join them. 'The merchant has a lot of money, and we'll go shares,' they told them. Every one of the five had a long knife in their hand each a knife. The innkeeper locked the door and said: 'Say your prayers, travellers, . . . and if you begin screaming,' they said, 'we won't let you say your prayers before you die. . . .' As though we could scream! I had such a lump in my throat I could not cry out. . . . The merchant wept and said: 'Good Christian people! you have resolved to kill me because my money tempts you. Well, so be it; I shall not be the first nor shall I be the last. Many of us merchants have been murdered at inns. But why, good Christian brothers,' says he, 'murder my driver? Why should he have to suffer for my money?' And he said that so pitifully! And the innkeeper answered him: 'If we leave him alive,' said he, 'he will be the first to bear witness against us. One may just as well kill two as one. You can but answer once for seven misdeeds. . . Say your prayers, that's all you can do, and it is no good talking!' The merchant and I knelt down side by side and wept and said our prayers. He thought of his children. I was young in those days; I wanted to live. . . . We looked at the images and prayed, and so pitifully that it brings a tear even now. . . . And the innkeeper's wife looks at us and says: 'Good people,' said she, 'don't bear a grudge against us in the other world and pray to God for our punishment, for it is want that drives us to it.' We prayed and wept and prayed and wept, and God heard us. He had pity on us, I suppose. . . . At the very minute when the innkeeper had taken the merchant by the beard to rip open his throat with his knife suddenly someone seemed to tap at the window from the yard! We all started, and the innkeeper's hands dropped. . . . Someone was tapping at the window and shouting: 'Pyotr Grigoritch,' he shouted, 'are you here? Get ready and let's go!' The people saw that someone had come for the merchant; they were terrified and took to their heels. . . . And we made haste into the yard, harnessed the horses, and were out of sight in a minute. . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Who was it knocked at the window?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "At the window? It must have been a holy saint or angel, for there was no one else. . . . When we drove out of the yard there wasn't a soul in the street. . . . It was the Lord's doing."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, over the open country. . . . He is coming this way."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And maybe it's the merchant who was buried here walking over the steppe,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's only those walk at night whom the earth will not take to herself. And the merchants were all right. . . . The merchants have received the crown of martyrs."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Just look what a smile I have!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A fine big bird; what did you kill it with?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Grape-shot. You can't get him with small shot, he won't let you get near enough. Buy it, friends! I will let you have it for twenty kopecks."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What use would it be to us? It's good roast, but I bet it would be tough boiled; you could not get your teeth into it. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, what a pity! I would take it to the gentry at the farm; they would give me half a rouble for it. But it's a long way to go-- twelve miles!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Konstantin Zvonik from Rovno. It's three miles from here."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do you live with your father or in a house of your own?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No; now I am living in a house of my own. I have parted. This month, just after St. Peter's Day, I got married. I am a married man now! . . . It's eighteen days since the wedding."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Marriage is a good thing . . . . God's blessing is on it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "His young wife sits at home while he rambles about the steppe,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But, Lord, she is not at home!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She is not; she has gone to her mother's for three days! Yes, indeed, she has gone away, and I feel as though I were not married. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She has gone to Demidovo to see her mother,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She'll be back to-morrow. . . . She said she would be back to dinner."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Lord, yes; I should think so. We have only been married such a little while, and she has gone away. . . . Eh! Oh, but she is a tricky one, God strike me dead! She is such a fine, splendid girl, such a one for laughing and singing, full of life and fire! When she is there your brain is in a whirl, and now she is away I wander about the steppe like a fool, as though I had lost something. I have been walking since dinner."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "such a housewife, clever and sensible. You wouldn't find another like her among simple folk in the whole province. She has gone away. . . . But she is missing me, I kno-ow! I know the little magpie. She said she would be back to-morrow by dinner-time. . . . And just think how queer!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Now she loves me and is sad without me, and yet she would not marry me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have been struggling with her for three years! I saw her at the Kalatchik fair; I fell madly in love with her, was ready to hang myself. . . . I live at Rovno, she at Demidovo, more than twenty miles apart, and there was nothing I could do. I sent match-makers to her, and all she said was: 'I won't!' Ah, the magpie! I sent her one thing and another, earrings and cakes, and twenty pounds of honey-- but still she said: 'I won't!' And there it was. If you come to think of it, I was not a match for her! She was young and lovely, full of fire, while I am old: I shall soon be thirty, and a regular beauty, too; a fine beard like a goat's, a clear complexion all covered with pimples-- how could I be compared with her! The only thing to be said is that we are well off, but then the Vahramenkys are well off, too. They've six oxen, and they keep a couple of labourers. I was in love, friends, as though I were plague-stricken. I couldn't sleep or eat; my brain was full of thoughts, and in such a maze, Lord preserve us! I longed to see her, and she was in Demidovo. What do you think? God be my witness, I am not lying, three times a week I walked over there on foot just to have a look at her. I gave up my work! I was so frantic that I even wanted to get taken on as a labourer in Demidovo, so as to be near her. I was in misery! My mother called in a witch a dozen times; my father tried thrashing me. For three years I was in this torment, and then I made up my mind. 'Damn my soul!' I said. 'I will go to the town and be a cabman. . . . It seems it is fated not to be.' At Easter I went to Demidovo to have a last look at her. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I saw her by the river with the lads,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I was overcome with anger. . . . I called her aside and maybe for a full hour I said all manner of things to her. She fell in love with me! For three years she did not like me! she fell in love with me for what I said to her. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What did I say? I don't remember. . . How could one remember? My words flowed at the time like water from a tap, without stopping to take breath. Ta-ta-ta! And now I can't utter a word. . . . Well, so she married me. . . . She's gone now to her mother's, the magpie, and while she is away here I wander over the steppe. I can't stay at home. It's more than I can do!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Our Mother Russia is the he-ad of all the world!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Thank you for your hospitality. I shall go on again towards that light. It's more than I can stand."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The Armenians live there. They are a good sort of people, . . . the Arnienians are."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He has sent a man to the settlement for some papers, and he doesn't come . . . . He should have sent Styopka."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is all right, a good man,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "God give him health -- a splendid gentleman, Semyon Alexandritch. . . . It's people like that the earth rests upon. That's true. . . . The cocks are not crowing yet, and he is already up and about. . . . Another man would be asleep, or gallivanting with visitors at home, but he is on the steppe all day, . . . on his rounds. . . . He does not let things slip. . . . No-o! He's a fine fellow. . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Allow us to send Styopka! Emelyan, call out that Styopka should be sent."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That must be one of his circuit men,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He must have a hundred such horsemen or maybe more."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's a pity he is so harsh! But he is all right, a good man. . . . He doesn't abuse men for nothing. . . . It's no matter. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Here he lolls, the lumpy face, and is the first to put his spoon in,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Greedy! always contrives to sit next the cauldron. He's been a church-singer, so he thinks he is a gentleman! There are a lot of singers like you begging along the highroad!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To teach you not to be the first to dip into the cauldron. Don't think too much of yourself!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are a fool, and that is all about it!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Anyone can sing like that-- sit in the church porch and sing 'Give me alms, for Christ's sake!' Ugh! you are a nice fellow!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I don't care to have anything to do with you, or I would show you what to think of yourself."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But why are you pushing me, you Mazeppa?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Eh! I am a Mazeppa? Yes? Take that, then; go and look for it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are the worst of the lot; I can't bear you!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In the next world you will burn in hell! I'll complain to Ivan Ivanitch. Don't you dare insult Emelyan!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "'every little sucking-pig wants to lay down the law.' Shall I pull your ear?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How dreary I am! O Lord! Don't you take offence, Emelyan,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A mat. There will be rain, so cover yourself up."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ah, my poor feet, how they ache!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Fill heaven and earth with Thy glory."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Get down! Is he deaf, the silly little thing? . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It was a good storm, all right, . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Thank God, . . . my feet are a little softened by the rain. It was all right. . . . Have you got down, Yegory? Well, go into the hut; it is all right. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "it must have struck something . . . . Are you of these parts?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, from Glinovo. We belong to Glinovo. We are working at the Platers'."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "All sorts. Just now we are getting in the wheat. The lightning, the lightning! It is long since we have had such a storm. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What a storm God has sent us!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And our lads are out for the night on the steppe; they'll have a bad time, poor dears! Take off your things, little sir, take off your things."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What's the use of standing there, with your legs apart, little lad?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Have something to eat, my dear! I have nothing else to offer you, . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Our lads are out on the steppe for the night, . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The terror of the Lord! I'd light the candle under the ikon, but I don't know where Stepanida has put it. Have some more, little sir, have some more. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "it will soon be time to get up. Our lads are out on the steppe for the night; they are all wet through for sure. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lord Jesus Christ! I was asleep, when I heard a noise as though someone were knocking. I woke up and looked, and it was the storm God had sent us. . . . I'd have lighted the candle, but I couldn't find it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If only nothing's struck in an unlucky hour. Our lads are out on the steppe for the night. Lie down and sleep, my dear. . . . Christ be with you, my child. . . . I won't take away the melon; maybe you'll have a bit when you get up."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The terror of the Lord! It thunders and thunders, and there is no end to it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "it's getting quieter. . . . The lads have gone into the huts, and two have stayed with the horses. The lads have. . . . They can't; . . . the horses would be taken away. . . . I'll sit here a bit and then go and take my turn. . . . We can't leave them; they would be taken. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Go to sleep, my child, go to sleep,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How dreary and comfortless to be a peasant!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Never mind, we shall soon be there,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He must have got a chill to the stomach. The little lad must. . . away from home; it's a bad lookout!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We arrived yesterday evening. . . . We have been expecting you all day. We meant to overtake you yesterday, but it was out of our way; we came by the other road. I say, how you have crumpled your coat! You'll catch it from your uncle!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your uncle and Father Christopher are in the inn now, drinking tea; come along!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ah, our gentleman that is to be,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, how did you like the journey, puer bone?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Sick of it, I've no doubt? God save us all from having to travel by waggon or with oxen. You go on and on, God forgive us; you look ahead and the steppe is always lying stretched out the same as it was-- you can't see the end of it! It's not travelling but regular torture. Why don't you drink your tea? Drink it up; and in your absence, while you have been trailing along with the waggons, we have settled all our business capitally. Thank God we have sold our wool to Tcherepahin, and no one could wish to have done better. . . . We have made a good bargain."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yegory, what is the matter with you? Why are you crying?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That's not the right thing, my boy. . . . One mustn't be ill on a journey. Aie, aie, what are you thinking about, boy . . . eh?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, your head's feverish. . . . You must have caught cold or else have eaten something. . . . Pray to God."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No; he ought to have something hot. . . . Yegory, have a little drop of soup? Eh?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I was chilly before, but now . . . now I am hot. And I ache all over. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I tell you what, you undress and go to bed,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He must be rubbed with oil and vinegar. Please God, he will be better to-morrow."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, take it! that's the way to do business!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If I could have known that Tcherepahin would give such a price,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wouldn't have sold Makarov those five tons at home. It is vexatious! But who could have told that the price had gone up here?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I think of going to the cathedral to-morrow,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I know the sacristan there. I ought to go and see the bishop after mass, but they say he is ill."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "So I shall go away without seeing him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lomonosov, are you asleep? Sit up; I'm going to rub you with oil and vinegar. It's a good thing, only you must say a prayer."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "lie with your back upwards-- that's it. . . . You'll be all right to-morrow, but don't do it again. . . . You are as hot as fire. I suppose you were on the road in the storm."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You might well fall ill! In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, . . . you might well fall ill!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "God has sent us blessings-- well, how are you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Thank God. . . . I have come from mass. I've been to see a sacristan I know. He invited me to breakfast with him, but I didn't go. I don't like visiting people too early, God bless them!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "See; I passed a fish-shop and brought this,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There is no need to indulge in luxuries on an ordinary weekday; but I thought, I've an invalid at home, so it is excusable. And the caviare is good, real sturgeon. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Eat now and enjoy yourself, but the time will soon come for you to be studying. Mind you study with attention and application, so that good may come of it. What you have to learn by heart, learn by heart, but when you have to tell the inner sense in your own words, without regard to the outer form, then say it in your own words. And try to master all subjects. One man knows mathematics excellently, but has never heard of Pyotr Mogila; another knows about Pyotr Mogila, but cannot explain about the moon. But you study so as to understand everything. Study Latin, French, German, . . . geography, of course, history, theology, philosophy, mathematics, . . . and when you have mastered everything, not with haste but with prayer and with zeal, then go into the service. When you know everything it will be easy for you in any line of life. . . . You study and strive for the divine blessing, and God will show you what to be. Whether a doctor, a judge or an engineer. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The Apostle Paul says: 'Do not apply yourself to strange and diverse studies.' Of course, if it is black magic, unlawful arts, or calling up spirits from the other world, like Saul, or studying subjects that can be of no use to yourself or others, better not learn them. You must undertake only what God has blessed. Take example . . . the Holy Apostles spoke in all languages, so you study languages. Basil the Great studied mathematics and philosophy-- so you study them; St. Nestor wrote history-- so you study and write history. Take example from the saints."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I was educated in the old-fashioned way; I have forgotten a great deal by now, but still I live differently from other people. Indeed, there is no comparison. For instance, in company at a dinner, or at an assembly, one says something in Latin, or makes some allusion from history or philosophy, and it pleases people, and it pleases me myself. . . . Or when the circuit court comes and one has to take the oath, all the other priests are shy, but I am quite at home with the judges, the prosecutors, and the lawyers. I talk intellectually, drink a cup of tea with them, laugh, ask them what I don't know, . . . and they like it. So that's how it is, my boy. Learning is light and ignorance is darkness. Study! It's hard, of course; nowadays study is expensive. . . . Your mother is a widow; she lives on her pension, but there, of course . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ivan Ivanitch will assist. He won't desert you. He has no children of his own, and he will help you. Don't be uneasy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Only mind, Yegory, don't forget your mother and Ivan Ivanitch, God preserve you from it. The commandment bids you honour your mother, and Ivan Ivanitch is your benefactor and takes the place of a father to you. If you become learned, God forbid you should be impatient and scornful with people because they are not so clever as you, then woe, woe to you!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, I have settled all our business,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We might have gone home to-day, but we have still to think about Yegor. We must arrange for him. My sister told me that Nastasya Petrovna, a friend of hers, lives somewhere here, so perhaps she will take him in as a boarder."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "'Little Lower Street: Nastasya Petrovna Toskunov, living in a house of her own.' We must go at once and try to find her. It's a nuisance!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are sticking to me like a burr. You and your mother want education and gentlemanly breeding and I have nothing but worry with you both. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "it's a long way off, out that way towards the town grazing ground."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There is no one called Toskunov here,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Excuse me, there's no one called Toskunov. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I tell you there isn't, and there isn't."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why, Nastasya Petrovna live in her own house now!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lord! it is eight years since she married her daughter and gave up the house to her son-in-law! It's her son-in-law lives there now."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How is it you didn't know a simple thing like that, you fools?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She moved ever so long ago! It's eight years since she gave up her house to her son-in-law! Upon my word!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Go straight on, straight on, straight on. You will pass a little red house, then you will see a little alley on your left. Turn down that little alley, and it will be the third gate on the right. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Tell me, please, does Nastasya Petrovna Toskunov live here?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes! But what do you want with her?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Very pleased to see you. . . . You see, your old friend Olga Ivanovna Knyasev sends her love to you. This is her little son. And I, perhaps you remember, am her brother Ivan Ivanitch. . . . You are one of us from N.. . . You were born among us and married there. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My own darling! Ah, holy saints, why am I standing here like a fool? My pretty little angel. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Olga's little boy! How delightful! He is his mother all over! The image of his mother! But why are you standing in the yard? Come indoors."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The room has not been done yet,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, Mother of God! Vassilisa, go and open the shutters anyway! My little angel! My little beauty! I did not know that Olitchka had a boy like that!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "if you will be so kind, and we will pay ten roubles a month for his keep. He is not a spoilt boy; he is quiet. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I really don't know what to say, Ivan Ivanitch!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ten roubles a month is very good, but it is a dreadful thing to take another person's child! He may fall ill or something. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, let him stay with you now, then,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't be troublesome; mind you obey Nastasya Petrovna. . . . Good-bye; I am coming again to-morrow."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We have no time for tea! We are just setting off."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mind you work hard. . . . Don't forget your mother, and obey Nastasya Petrovna. . . . If you are diligent at school, Yegor, I'll stand by you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. . . . Study,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Work hard, my lad. If I die, remember me in your prayers. Here is a ten-kopeck piece from me, too. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have applied at the high school already,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You will take him for the entrance examination on the seventh of August. . . . Well, good-bye; God bless you, good-bye, Yegor!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You might at least have had a cup of tea,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown
